title: Mihin and minne: answering with common into-forms
summary: Mihin and minne ask for a destination. Mihin sinä menet? — Menen kouluun.
targetSkills: Mihin and minne: answering with common into-forms
objectives: Ask for a destination with mihin or minne.
Answer using the taught common into-forms.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern.
The illative is an into/to form; mihin aikaan uses that form in a time expression.
Mihin and minne ask for a destination. Both can mean where to. These examples use a bounded set of common illatives, the forms meaning into a place: kouluun, taloon, kahvilaan and kirjastoon.
keyPoints: Mihin/minne ask where to, rather than where someone is or comes from.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: For these nouns, repeat the final stem vowel and add n: koulu + u + n gives kouluun (“to school”). The answer can be Kouluun or Menen kouluun (“I am going to school”). This lesson does not claim that every Finnish noun forms its illative this way.
A natural short reply to “Mihin sinä menet?” is “Kouluun.” (“To school.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
The supplied negative phrase en mene rejects the suggested destination. Give the actual destination afterwards; both destinations retain their into-forms.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Use the taught into-form for the destination, not a location or source form.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: kouluun means to school here. Repeat the final u of koulu and add n: koulu + u + n gives kouluun.
kahvilaan means to the cafe here. Repeat the final a and add n: kahvila + a + n gives kahvilaan.
kirjastoon means to the library here. Repeat the final o and add n: kirjasto + o + n gives kirjastoon.
metsään means into the forest here. Repeat final ä and add n: metsä + ä + n gives metsään.
halliin means into the hall here. Repeat the final i and add n: halli + i + n gives halliin.
taloon means into the house here. Repeat the final o of talo and add n: talo + o + n gives taloon.
keyPoints: Use the taught into-form for the destination, not a location or source form.

steps: Mihin: where to; question asking where to. Mihin is the illative question form; in mihin aikaan it instead asks at what time.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
menet: you go; verb (the action or state). Mene- + singular second-person -t gives menet.
Menen: I go; verb (the action or state). Mennä removes -nä and adds e to form mene-, then adds -n: menen.
kouluun: to school; destination. Repeat the final u of koulu and add n: koulu + u + n gives kouluun.
Mihin: where to; question asking where to. Mihin is the illative question form; in mihin aikaan it instead asks at what time.
hän: he or she; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Hän refers to one other person without specifying gender.
menee: goes; verb (the action or state). Lengthen the final e of mene-: menee.

steps: En: I do not; negative verb (marks not and identifies the person). En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.
mene: go; main verb after the negative verb. Remove -n from menen to obtain negative mene, unchanged after every present negative verb.
